summary: Sarah dies in Canaan, and Abraham mourns her, then tells the children of Heth that he is a foreigner seeking a burial possession. In a public negotiation he insists on paying Ephron for the field and cave of Machpelah; after the silver is weighed and the property deeded, he buries Sarah there.
whyItMatters: The first specified land holding in this ancestral story is a grave acquired through an acknowledged purchase. Sarah’s death and Abraham’s resident-foreigner status make the transaction more than a simple real-estate report.

context.author: Genesis names no historical writer. Jewish and Christian tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the book briefing describes older traditions shaped into a final literary form, without a settled account of every stage.
context.audience: The book addresses Israel through a story of shared human origins and the family from whom Israel traces its ancestry; no single first audience is named in this chapter.
context.date: The narrated events belong to primeval or ancestral time, not to a securely dated writing event. Major stages of Genesis are often placed across the monarchic to Persian periods, with exact models and dates debated.
context.setting: Kiriath Arba or Hebron, at the city gate and the field and cave of Machpelah.
context.literaryForm: Death and mourning notice followed by public land negotiation, transfer formula, and burial.

before.text: Abraham returns from the test involving Isaac, and the chapter closes by naming Rebekah in his brother’s family. The narrative next turns to Sarah’s death.

here.text: Follow Abraham’s mourning and how he secures one burial place through public discussion and payment while calling himself a foreigner.

after.text: Abraham sends his senior servant to seek a wife for Isaac among relatives, setting the next household transition in motion.

outline.heading: Sarah dies; Abraham mourns
outline.note: Sarah’s death at Hebron and Abraham’s grief begin the scene.

outline.heading: A foreigner asks for burial land
outline.note: Abraham asks the children of Heth and specifies Ephron’s cave for full price.

outline.heading: Public offer and stated price
outline.note: Ephron speaks at the city gate and names four hundred shekels.

outline.heading: Payment, deed, and burial
outline.note: Abraham weighs silver, receives the field and cave, and buries Sarah.

keyVerses.text: “I am a stranger and a foreigner living with you. Give me a possession of a burying-place with you, that I may bury my dead out of my sight.”
keyVerses.why: Abraham describes himself as a resident foreigner when requesting a burial possession.

keyVerses.text: Abraham listened to Ephron. Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver which he had named in the hearing of the children of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, according to the current merchants’ standard.
keyVerses.why: The weighed silver and public witness anchor the land transfer in an actual purchase.

keyVerses.text: After this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah before Mamre (that is, Hebron), in the land of Canaan.
keyVerses.why: Sarah’s burial is the purpose for which the field and cave were acquired.

questions.question: What happens to Sarah in this chapter?
questions.answer: She dies at Kiriath Arba, also called Hebron, and Abraham comes to mourn and weep for her. The rest of the chapter concerns a place to bury her, not an account of her final words or cause of death.

questions.question: What does Abraham mean by “stranger and foreigner”?
questions.answer: He lives among the children of Heth without already holding the burial ground he needs. Calling himself a foreigner helps explain why he seeks a recognized possession through their public consent and payment.

questions.question: Why does Abraham insist on paying when Ephron offers the land?
questions.answer: He asks for the cave and field for the full price and then weighs the silver Ephron states before the local witnesses. The chapter emphasizes a documented transaction that can serve as a secure burial possession.

questions.question: What is a “shekel” here?
questions.answer: It is the silver weight used to state Ephron’s price, four hundred shekels, according to a merchants’ standard. The text reports Abraham weighing it; it does not give a modern currency conversion.

questions.question: Does this purchase prove Abraham already possesses all of Canaan?
questions.answer: No. He obtains a particular field, cave, and trees in a public transaction while describing himself as a foreign resident. The broader land promise remains distinct from this limited burial holding.

questions.question: Who witnesses the transfer?
questions.answer: The negotiations occur before the children of Heth and people entering the city gate. The text repeats their presence when the field and cave are deeded to Abraham.

questions.question: Why does a burial place matter within the promise story?
questions.answer: Sarah is buried in Canaan, but Abraham must purchase the site while he remains a foreigner. The narrative places death, rootedness, and the not-yet-fulfilled land promise alongside one another.

questions.question: What is Machpelah?
questions.answer: It is the named field and cave before Mamre near Hebron that Abraham purchases from Ephron. The cave becomes Sarah’s burial place in the closing lines.

glossary.def: The field and cave bought from Ephron for Sarah’s burial near Hebron.
Weights of silver used to state and pay Ephron’s price for the burial property.
Transferred as an acknowledged possession before the local witnesses.
